name: ServiceAccounts & least-privilege RBAC
objective: CKA › Cluster Architecture, Installation & Configuration. Drill EVERY RBAC corner harder than the exam: namespaced Role vs cluster-scoped ClusterRole, binding to users and ServiceAccounts, reusing a ClusterRole inside one namespace via a RoleBinding, least-privilege with resourceNames, apiGroups for subresources, approving a CSR, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: ServiceAccount identity
questions.teach:
**ServiceAccounts** are identities for workloads, not humans. You grant one permissions the same way — bind a Role to it with a RoleBinding. The CLI shortcut uses a colon: `--serviceaccount=<ns>:<name>`.

**Gotcha:** in `auth can-i --as=` the SA is the full form `system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>`, not the short `ns:name` used on the binding flag.
questions.prompt:
In `rbac-learn`, create a ServiceAccount `ci`, then create a RoleBinding `ci-pr` binding the existing `pod-reader` Role to it.

Target: `kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:rbac-learn:ci -n rbac-learn` → `yes`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n rbac-learn create sa ci`, then `kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding ci-pr --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=rbac-learn:ci`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n rbac-learn create sa ci
kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding ci-pr --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=rbac-learn:ci
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:rbac-learn:ci -n rbac-learn   # -> yes

verification.description: ServiceAccount ci exists and is bound to pod-reader; the SA identity can list pods in rbac-learn

questions.eli5:
People log into the cluster as *users*, but the programs running inside the cluster (your pods) need an identity too — they can't type a password. A **ServiceAccount** is a badge made for a *robot worker* instead of a person. A CI job, an operator, a controller — each can carry its own ServiceAccount badge.

Here's the nice part: you grant a ServiceAccount permissions **exactly the same way** you grant a human. You bind a Role to it with a RoleBinding. The only difference is how you name it.

On the binding command, the shortcut spelling uses a colon: `--serviceaccount=rbac-learn:ci` — that's `<namespace>:<name>`.

But when you *test* it with `auth can-i --as=`, you must use the robot's full official name: `system:serviceaccount:rbac-learn:ci`. That long form is the real username Kubernetes uses internally for every ServiceAccount. The short `ns:name` is just a convenience the `create rolebinding` command accepts.

So: make the SA (`create sa ci`), bind the existing `pod-reader` Role to it, then verify with the long `--as=system:serviceaccount:...` form.

**Watch out for:**

- **Two different spellings for the same SA.** The binding flag takes `rbac-learn:ci`; `--as=` needs the full `system:serviceaccount:rbac-learn:ci`. Mixing them up is the classic trap.
- A ServiceAccount is **namespaced** — `ci` in `rbac-learn` is a different identity from `ci` in `default`.
- Creating the SA alone grants **nothing** — you still need the RoleBinding, just like with users.
- Every namespace has a `default` SA that pods use unless you set `serviceAccountName`. Prefer a dedicated, least-privilege SA for each workload.
questions.deepDive:
## ServiceAccount identity + RBAC — full rundown

### The mental model
A **ServiceAccount (SA)** is an in-cluster identity for **workloads** (pods), the way a User is an identity for humans. SAs are **namespaced objects**, created by the API. You authorize an SA exactly like a user — bind a Role/ClusterRole to it with a (Cluster)RoleBinding. The only wrinkle is the **two naming forms**: the binding flag uses `<ns>:<name>`, but the SA's real username (used in impersonation and tokens) is `system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>`.

### The two name forms (memorize this)
| Context | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `create rolebinding --serviceaccount=` | `<ns>:<name>` | `rbac-learn:ci` |
| `auth can-i --as=` / token subject / YAML `subjects` | `system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>` | `system:serviceaccount:rbac-learn:ci` |
| Every SA is also in group | `system:serviceaccounts` and `system:serviceaccounts:<ns>` | — |

### Commands
```bash
# create the ServiceAccount
kubectl -n rbac-learn create sa ci

# bind an existing Role to it (note the colon form)
kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding ci-pr \
  --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=rbac-learn:ci

# test with the FULL username form
kubectl auth can-i list pods \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:rbac-learn:ci -n rbac-learn      # -> yes
```

### Equivalent YAML binding
```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: ci-pr
  namespace: rbac-learn
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount          # note: NO apiGroup for a ServiceAccount subject
  name: ci
  namespace: rbac-learn
```
> Subject nuance: a `ServiceAccount` subject uses `kind: ServiceAccount` + `name` + `namespace` and **no `apiGroup`**. A `User`/`Group` subject uses `apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io` and no namespace.

### Using the SA from a pod
```yaml
spec:
  serviceAccountName: ci        # pod runs as SA "ci"; token auto-mounted
```
- A projected token is mounted at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token`.
- If unset, the pod uses the namespace's **`default`** SA.
- Get a token manually: `kubectl -n rbac-learn create token ci` (TokenRequest API, short-lived).
- Disable auto-mount with `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the SA or pod.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **The two name forms differ.** Binding flag = `rbac-learn:ci`; `--as=` = `system:serviceaccount:rbac-learn:ci`. This trips up almost everyone.
- SAs are **namespaced** — `ci` in one namespace ≠ `ci` in another; the subject must name the SA's own namespace.
- Creating the SA grants **nothing** — you still need the binding.
- In a YAML subject, do **not** put `apiGroup` on a `ServiceAccount` (it's the empty core group); do put `namespace`.
- Pods without `serviceAccountName` silently use `default` — least privilege means giving each workload its own SA.
- Modern clusters don't auto-create a long-lived Secret token per SA; use `kubectl create token` or a projected volume.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n rbac-learn create sa ci
kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding ci-pr --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=rbac-learn:ci
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:rbac-learn:ci -n rbac-learn   # yes
```

questions.title: Reuse a ClusterRole inside one namespace
questions.teach:
A **RoleBinding** can reference a **ClusterRole** instead of a Role — reusing the ClusterRole's rules but scoping the grant to the RoleBinding's **own namespace only**. (`deployments` live in the `apps` apiGroup.)

**Gotcha:** the subject gets the permissions **only in that namespace**, never cluster-wide.
questions.prompt:
In `rbac-learn`, create a ClusterRole `deploy-admin` allowing `get,list,create,update,delete` on `deployments` (apps apiGroup), then create a **RoleBinding** `dev-deploy` in `rbac-learn` that grants that ClusterRole to user `dev` (namespace-scoped reuse).

Target: `can-i create deployments --as=dev -n rbac-learn` → `yes`, but `can-i create deployments --as=dev -n default` → `no`.
questions.hint: `kubectl create clusterrole deploy-admin --verb=get,list,create,update,delete --resource=deployments.apps`, then `kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding dev-deploy --clusterrole=deploy-admin --user=dev`.
questions.solution:
kubectl create clusterrole deploy-admin --verb=get,list,create,update,delete --resource=deployments.apps
kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding dev-deploy --clusterrole=deploy-admin --user=dev
kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as=dev -n rbac-learn   # -> yes
kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as=dev -n default      # -> no

verification.description: RoleBinding dev-deploy references ClusterRole deploy-admin (apps group); dev can create deployments in rbac-learn but NOT in default

questions.eli5:
A **ClusterRole** is a job description written on building-wide letterhead. Normally you'd hand it out with a building-wide hire letter (a ClusterRoleBinding), and the person could do that job in *every room*. But sometimes that's too much power.

Neat trick: you can take that same building-wide job description and hand it out with a **room-local hire letter** — a plain **RoleBinding** inside one room. The person gets the ClusterRole's powers, but *only in that one room*. Same job description, deliberately leashed to a single namespace.

Why reuse a ClusterRole this way instead of writing a Role? Because you write the rules **once** and reuse them in many namespaces, each scoped locally. It's the standard pattern behind the built-in `admin`, `edit`, and `view` roles.

So here: the rules ("manage deployments") live in a ClusterRole `deploy-admin`. You bind it to `dev` with a **RoleBinding** in `rbac-learn`. Now `dev` can create deployments in `rbac-learn` — but ask the same question in `default` and the answer is `no`, because the leash only covers `rbac-learn`.

One more thing: deployments aren't in the "core" group — they live in the **`apps`** apiGroup. On the command line you write that as `deployments.apps`.

**Watch out for:**

- **RoleBinding → ClusterRole scopes the grant to that one namespace only.** Never cluster-wide. That's the whole point here.
- Use `--clusterrole=` (not `--role=`) on the RoleBinding when referencing a ClusterRole.
- Deployments are `apps` group — `--resource=deployments.apps` (or they just won't match).
- The binding's namespace is what matters: in `rbac-learn` it works, in `default` it doesn't.
- The ClusterRole still grants nothing until some binding references it.
questions.deepDive:
## Reuse a ClusterRole inside one namespace — full rundown

### The mental model
A **ClusterRole** holds reusable rules. How far those rules reach depends on the **binding**, not the ClusterRole:
- **ClusterRoleBinding → ClusterRole** = permissions **cluster-wide** (all namespaces + cluster-scoped resources).
- **RoleBinding → ClusterRole** = the *same rules*, but **confined to the RoleBinding's own namespace**.

This "write rules once, scope per namespace" pattern is why Kubernetes ships `admin`/`edit`/`view` as ClusterRoles you attach with RoleBindings.

### The scoping matrix
| Binding | References | Effective scope |
|---|---|---|
| RoleBinding → **Role** | Role in same ns | that namespace |
| RoleBinding → **ClusterRole** | any ClusterRole | **that namespace only** |
| ClusterRoleBinding → **ClusterRole** | any ClusterRole | **cluster-wide** |

### apiGroups — where resources live
Deployments are **not** in the core group. You must name the group.
| Resource | apiGroup | CLI shorthand |
|---|---|---|
| pods, services, configmaps, secrets | `""` (core) | `pods` |
| deployments, replicasets, daemonsets, statefulsets | `apps` | `deployments.apps` |
| jobs, cronjobs | `batch` | `jobs.batch` |
| ingresses, networkpolicies | `networking.k8s.io` | `ingresses.networking.k8s.io` |
| roles, rolebindings | `rbac.authorization.k8s.io` | `roles.rbac.authorization.k8s.io` |

### Commands
```bash
# ClusterRole with the reusable rules (deployments are in apps)
kubectl create clusterrole deploy-admin \
  --verb=get,list,create,update,delete --resource=deployments.apps

# RoleBinding IN rbac-learn referencing the ClusterRole -> scoped to rbac-learn
kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding dev-deploy \
  --clusterrole=deploy-admin --user=dev

# verify the scoping
kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as=dev -n rbac-learn   # -> yes
kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as=dev -n default      # -> no
```

### Equivalent YAML
```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: deploy-admin
rules:
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments"]
  verbs: ["get","list","create","update","delete"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding               # RoleBinding, not ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: dev-deploy
  namespace: rbac-learn         # <-- this namespace is the scope
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole             # <-- referencing a ClusterRole
  name: deploy-admin
subjects:
- apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: User
  name: dev
```

### Why it stays namespaced
A RoleBinding only ever grants within **its own namespace**, regardless of whether its roleRef is a Role or a ClusterRole. The ClusterRole merely supplies the *rules*; the RoleBinding supplies the *reach*. The rules themselves can only touch namespaced resources when applied this way — cluster-scoped resources named in the ClusterRole are **not** granted through a RoleBinding.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **RoleBinding → ClusterRole is namespace-scoped, never cluster-wide.** Verify with a second `can-i` in a different namespace returning `no`.
- Use **`--clusterrole=`** (not `--role=`) on the RoleBinding when the target is a ClusterRole.
- **Deployments are `apps`** — `--resource=deployments.apps`; omitting the group can match nothing or the wrong resource.
- Cluster-scoped resources in the ClusterRole are **not** honored via a RoleBinding — only namespaced ones.
- The scoping comes from the **RoleBinding's namespace**, so create it with the right `-n`.
- ClusterRole still needs a binding; rules alone grant nothing.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl create clusterrole deploy-admin --verb=get,list,create,update,delete --resource=deployments.apps
kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding dev-deploy --clusterrole=deploy-admin --user=dev
kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as=dev -n rbac-learn   # yes
kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as=dev -n default      # no
```

questions.title: Least privilege with resourceNames
questions.teach:
Least privilege can go below resource level: `resourceNames` restricts a rule to **specific named objects** — e.g. `get` only `app-config`, not every ConfigMap. CLI: `--resource-name=app-config` (repeatable).

**Gotcha:** `resourceNames` only works for verbs targeting a named object (`get`,`update`,`patch`,`delete`) — it can't restrict `list`, `watch`, or `create`.
questions.prompt:
Two ConfigMaps exist in `rbac-learn`: `app-config` and `other-config`. Create a Role `cm-reader` + RoleBinding `dev-cm` so user `dev` can `get` **only** `app-config`.

Target: `can-i get configmaps/app-config --as=dev -n rbac-learn` → `yes`, but `can-i get configmaps/other-config --as=dev -n rbac-learn` → `no`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n rbac-learn create role cm-reader --verb=get --resource=configmaps --resource-name=app-config`, then bind it to `dev`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n rbac-learn create role cm-reader --verb=get --resource=configmaps --resource-name=app-config
kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding dev-cm --role=cm-reader --user=dev
kubectl auth can-i get configmaps/app-config  --as=dev -n rbac-learn   # -> yes
kubectl auth can-i get configmaps/other-config --as=dev -n rbac-learn   # -> no

verification.description: Role cm-reader restricted via resourceNames; dev can get app-config but NOT other-config

questions.eli5:
Usually a permission says "you may read **configmaps**" — meaning *all* of them in the room. But sometimes you want to be stingier: "you may read **only this one specific configmap**, named `app-config`, and nothing else." That extra-tight leash is what **`resourceNames`** does — it pins a rule down to specific named objects instead of the whole type.

Think of a filing cabinet full of folders. Normal RBAC gives you a key to the whole cabinet. `resourceNames` instead gives you a key that only opens **one labeled folder** — `app-config` — while `other-config` stays locked.

On the command line it's `--resource-name=app-config` (and you can repeat it for several named objects).

But there's a sharp edge. `resourceNames` only makes sense for actions that operate on **one object you already name**: `get`, `update`, `patch`, `delete`. It **cannot** restrict `list`, `watch`, or `create`. Why? Because when you *list*, you're asking "show me everything" — there's no single name to match against yet. And when you *create*, the object doesn't exist yet, so there's nothing to name. So you can't say "list only app-config" — that's not a thing.

So here: a Role that allows `get` on configmaps, narrowed to `resourceNames: [app-config]`. Bind it to `dev`. Now `get app-config` → yes, `get other-config` → no.

**Watch out for:**

- **`resourceNames` doesn't work with `list`, `watch`, or `create`** — only with verbs that target one named object (`get`, `update`, `patch`, `delete`).
- If you grant `list`, the user can see **all** objects of that type — `resourceNames` can't hide the others from a list.
- The names are **exact strings** — `app-config` ≠ `App-Config`.
- `get <specific name>` works, but a bare `get configmaps` (which lists) may be denied — that's expected.
questions.deepDive:
## Least privilege with resourceNames — full rundown

### The mental model
Normally an RBAC rule grants a verb on an **entire resource type** in a namespace. **`resourceNames`** narrows a rule to **specific, named instances** of that resource — e.g. `get` on *only* the ConfigMap `app-config`, not every ConfigMap. It's the finest-grained lever in RBAC. Critically, it only applies to verbs that act on a **single, already-named object**.

### Which verbs resourceNames can restrict
| Verb | Works with resourceNames? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `get` | ✅ | targets one named object |
| `update` | ✅ | targets one named object |
| `patch` | ✅ | targets one named object |
| `delete` | ✅ | targets one named object |
| `list` | ❌ | returns a collection; no name to match |
| `watch` | ❌ | streams a collection; no name to match |
| `create` | ❌ | name doesn't exist yet at admission |
| `deletecollection` | ❌ | operates on a collection |

> A rule that pairs `list`/`watch`/`create` with `resourceNames` is effectively **broken** for those verbs — they are evaluated as if no name restriction applied / won't be authorized as intended. Keep named-object verbs in a **separate rule** from collection verbs.

### Commands
```bash
# Role: get, restricted to a specific object name
kubectl -n rbac-learn create role cm-reader \
  --verb=get --resource=configmaps --resource-name=app-config

# repeat --resource-name for multiple named objects:
#   --resource-name=app-config --resource-name=db-config

kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding dev-cm \
  --role=cm-reader --user=dev

# verify
kubectl auth can-i get configmaps/app-config   --as=dev -n rbac-learn   # -> yes
kubectl auth can-i get configmaps/other-config --as=dev -n rbac-learn   # -> no
```

### Equivalent YAML
```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: cm-reader
  namespace: rbac-learn
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["configmaps"]
  resourceNames: ["app-config"]       # only this named object
  verbs: ["get"]                      # get/update/patch/delete only
```

### Splitting rules (common real-world shape)
When you need to *list* the collection but only *modify* one object, use **two rules**:
```yaml
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["configmaps"]
  verbs: ["list","watch"]             # see all (no resourceNames possible)
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["configmaps"]
  resourceNames: ["app-config"]
  verbs: ["get","update","patch"]     # modify only this one
```

### How can-i evaluates it
`kubectl auth can-i get configmaps/app-config` checks a rule matching resource `configmaps` + verb `get` whose `resourceNames` includes `app-config` (or is empty = all). `other-config` isn't in the list, so no rule allows it → `no`.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **resourceNames ignores `list`, `watch`, `create`.** Don't expect "list only app-config" — impossible; a list grant exposes the whole collection.
- Combining `list` + `resourceNames` in one rule is a classic mistake — the name restriction is meaningless there.
- Names are **exact and case-sensitive**; a typo silently denies.
- To both list and restrict modifications, write **two separate rules**.
- `resourceNames` is still **namespaced** inside a Role — it names objects in that one namespace.
- Subresources can be named too (e.g. `pods` with `resourceNames: [web-0]` + verb `get` on `pods/log` requires naming the parent pod).

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n rbac-learn create role cm-reader --verb=get --resource=configmaps --resource-name=app-config
kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding dev-cm --role=cm-reader --user=dev
kubectl auth can-i get configmaps/app-config   --as=dev -n rbac-learn   # yes
kubectl auth can-i get configmaps/other-config --as=dev -n rbac-learn   # no
```

questions.title: Grant a subresource (pods/log)
questions.teach:
Some verbs target a **subresource**, written `resource/subresource` — e.g. reading logs is `get` on `pods/log`. In a Role rule, list it under `resources` alongside (or instead of) the parent. CLI: `--resource=pods/log`.

**Gotcha:** `get pods` does **not** imply `get pods/log` — the subresource is a separate rule entry.
questions.prompt:
In `rbac-learn`, create a Role `log-reader` allowing `get` on `pods/log`, and a RoleBinding `dev-log` granting it to user `dev`.

Target: `kubectl auth can-i get pods/log --as=dev -n rbac-learn` → `yes`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n rbac-learn create role log-reader --verb=get --resource=pods/log`, then `kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding dev-log --role=log-reader --user=dev`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n rbac-learn create role log-reader --verb=get --resource=pods/log
kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding dev-log --role=log-reader --user=dev
kubectl auth can-i get pods/log --as=dev -n rbac-learn   # -> yes

verification.description: Role log-reader grants get on pods/log bound to dev; dev can get pods/log

questions.eli5:
Some Kubernetes objects have "side doors" attached to them — extra things you can reach *through* the main object. A pod's **logs** are like that: they're not a separate object you list on their own, they hang off the pod as a sub-thing. Kubernetes calls these **subresources**, and you write them as `parent/subresource` — so pod logs are **`pods/log`**.

Here's the catch that surprises everyone: permission on the parent does **not** flow down to the side door. Being allowed to `get pods` does **not** mean you're allowed to `get pods/log`. They're graded separately. If you want someone to read logs, you have to grant `get` on `pods/log` as its own thing — list it right alongside (or instead of) `pods` in the Role's resources.

On the command line that's `--resource=pods/log`.

Think of a hotel room (the pod) and its safe (the log). Having a key to the room doesn't open the safe — the safe needs its own key.

So here: a Role allowing `get` on `pods/log`, bound to `dev`. Now `kubectl logs` works for `dev` because `get pods/log` is allowed.

**Watch out for:**

- **Parent access does NOT imply subresource access.** `get pods` ≠ `get pods/log`. You must grant the subresource explicitly.
- Subresources are written `resource/subresource` — `pods/log`, `pods/exec`, `pods/status`, `deployments/scale`.
- `kubectl logs` actually needs `get` on `pods/log` (to read logs it also typically needs `get` on the pod itself to find it — grant both if a learner can't even locate the pod).
- Common exam subresources: `pods/log` (logs), `pods/exec` (shell in), `pods/portforward`, `deployments/scale` (scaling), `*/status`.
questions.deepDive:
## Granting a subresource (pods/log) — full rundown

### The mental model
A **subresource** is an API endpoint attached to a parent object, addressed as **`resource/subresource`** (e.g. `pods/log`). In RBAC, a subresource is a **distinct resource**: permission on the parent does **not** cascade to it. To allow `kubectl logs`, you grant the verb on `pods/log` explicitly — it's a separate `resources` entry, not something `get pods` includes.

### Common subresources on the exam
| Subresource | Backs the action | Typical verb |
|---|---|---|
| `pods/log` | `kubectl logs` | `get` |
| `pods/exec` | `kubectl exec` | `create` |
| `pods/attach` | `kubectl attach` | `create` |
| `pods/portforward` | `kubectl port-forward` | `create` |
| `pods/status` | read/update pod status | `get`,`patch`,`update` |
| `pods/ephemeralcontainers` | `kubectl debug` | `update`,`patch` |
| `deployments/scale` | `kubectl scale` | `get`,`update`,`patch` |
| `deployments/status` | controller status | `get`,`patch` |
| `nodes/proxy` | kubelet/metrics proxy | `get`,`create` |

> Note the verbs: `pods/log` and `*/status` use `get`; `pods/exec`, `pods/attach`, `pods/portforward` use **`create`** (they open a connection), which surprises people.

### Commands
```bash
# Role granting get on the pods/log subresource
kubectl -n rbac-learn create role log-reader \
  --verb=get --resource=pods/log

kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding dev-log \
  --role=log-reader --user=dev

# verify
kubectl auth can-i get pods/log --as=dev -n rbac-learn   # -> yes
```

### Equivalent YAML
```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: log-reader
  namespace: rbac-learn
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods/log"]        # the subresource is its own entry
  verbs: ["get"]
```
To let someone *find* the pod **and** read its logs, grant both:
```yaml
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
  verbs: ["get","list"]          # list pods + get their logs
```

### Why the split exists
The API server treats `pods` and `pods/log` as separate authorization resources so you can grant log-reading without granting the ability to read/modify the pod spec (which can contain env vars, mounts, etc.), and vice versa. This is a least-privilege feature, not an inconsistency.

### How can-i resolves it
`kubectl auth can-i get pods/log` looks for a rule with resource `pods/log` + verb `get`. A rule granting only `pods` (no `/log`) does **not** match → `no`. The slash form must appear literally in the rule's `resources`.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Parent ≠ subresource.** `get pods` does not grant `get pods/log`. Add the subresource explicitly.
- `kubectl logs` typically needs **`get pods/log`** (and often `get pods` to locate the pod) — if a user can't read logs, check both.
- **Exec/attach/portforward use the verb `create`**, not `get`.
- Subresources are namespaced like their parent (within a Role).
- You can combine with `resourceNames` to scope logs to specific pods (name the **parent** pod).
- `apiGroups` for `pods/log` is the core group `[""]`; for `deployments/scale` it's `["apps"]`.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n rbac-learn create role log-reader --verb=get --resource=pods/log
kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding dev-log --role=log-reader --user=dev
kubectl auth can-i get pods/log --as=dev -n rbac-learn   # yes
# exec needs CREATE on pods/exec:
# kubectl create role shell --verb=create --resource=pods/exec
```
